title: Politeness and invitations
goal: Invite, accept and decline gracefully — and meet the biggest cultural gap between Estonia and many other cultures: a language with **almost no levels of politeness**.
bekal: use the conditional *-ksin* to soften requests
invite, accept and decline without sounding stiff

notes: ⚠️ **This is the biggest cultural adjustment for readers of this module.** Everyday Estonian has no "Sir", "Madam", "Mr", "Mrs" or "Professor" in address. Estonians call lecturers, bosses, in-laws and eighty-year-old neighbors **by first name only**. This isn't rudeness; adding a title actually feels stiff and distancing.

**Tahaksid, tuleksin, peaksin, teeksin, sobiks, oleks** — six conditional forms in one dialogue. It's used to soften, not to imagine. *Kas sa tahad?* (Do you want?) sounds direct; *Kas sa tahaksid?* (Would you like?) sounds like an offer.
**Hea meelega** — "with pleasure". Literally "with a good mind". It's the warmest way to accept an invitation.

⚠️ **Ei ole vaja** means "no need", and Estonians mean it. In some cultures a host's "please don't go to any trouble" still calls for a gift. In Estonia, *ei ole vaja* means exactly what it says. Bringing something is still welcome, but bringing nothing is perfectly normal too.

grammars.title: The conditional — -ksin
body: You've been using it since unit 5 (*ma sooviksin*) without taking it apart. Here is the full form.
after: **Negating it** uses the third-row form for everyone, just like ordinary negation: *ma ei tahaks*, *sa ei tahaks*, *nad ei tahaks*. Once again, Estonian negatives take less memorizing than the positive forms.
**Two uses:** softening requests (*kas sa saaksid aidata?* — could you help?) and imagining (*kui ma oleksin rikas* — if I were rich).
⚠️ Don't overuse it. Estonian doesn't soften sentences as often as English does. One conditional in a request is enough; three sound hesitant.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Sina or teie — and why the list is so short
body: Estonian has **two** levels of address. Some languages have a dozen. That means you have far less to think about — but also far less to show respect with.
after: **Estonians switch to *sina* very quickly** — often within the first conversation, and almost always at work. If in doubt, start with *teie* and wait; the other person will usually offer *sina* themselves. The phrases: *Räägime sina!* or *Kas me võiksime sinatada?*

⚠️ **There are no honorific titles.** *Härra* (Mr) and *proua* (Mrs) exist in the dictionary, but in daily life they're hardly used except in formal letters. Calling someone "Härra Tamm" in ordinary conversation sounds like a joke.

It takes getting used to, and it's fine if it feels strange for a few months. What matters: **using a first name is not a sign of disrespect.** In Estonia respect is shown by listening and being on time, not by choice of address.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Ma annan teada* ("I'll let you know") **means you will really let them know**. In many cultures a sentence like this is a gentle way of saying no; in Estonia it's understood as a promise. If you mean no, say no — *kahjuks ma ei saa* is already completely polite.

sections.title: ⚠️ Estonian politeness, and what it doesn't say

blocks.text: Most misunderstandings between newcomers and Estonians aren't about vocabulary. They're about what counts as polite, and the cultures happen to disagree at several points.

blocks.title: And the other way round — what you need to adjust
items: **Don't repeat an offer three times.** If someone declines food or help, once is enough. Repeating is seen as pressure, not hospitality.
**Don't say "yes" to things that aren't certain.** Reliability is valued far more than the wish to please.
**Don't fill every pause.** If a conversation stops for a moment, nothing is wrong. Talking on to fill the silence actually feels pushy.
**Arrive on time, or let them know beforehand.** One short message saves the whole impression.
Would you like to come over?
